"I am often asked why I am so adamantly opposed to the War on Drugs
and why I am so outspoken about it." A Remarkable Insight from A Reader

March 22, 1999

Mr. Cowan,

I am often asked why I am so adamantly opposed to the War on Drugs and why I am so outspoken about it.

Aside from the obvious reasons of logic and the rights of the People I have a deeper, more personal reason.

In 1988 I joined the United States Navy. Many factors motivated this decision; money for college, ‘three hot and a cot,’ and simple patriotism. I was 18.

In October of 1990 my ship, the USS Crommelin (FFG-37) deployed to Central and South America for "Law enforcement operations." Put in civilian terms, we were looking for drug smugglers. We stopped numerous ships. Drugs were found only on the Crommelin. (The ship made a port visit to Jamaica and a crewman couldn’t wait to partake until after the cloud of suspicion was gone that generally hung over the ship when we left a "drug" port, i.e. Jamaica, Thailand.)

We were also charged with finding aircraft that fit a certain profile. 

As an Operations Specialist, my primary duty was as a radar operator. One December night in 1990 as we steamed off the coast of Panama I was tracking air contacts when I detected one that fit the profile I was given. I reported it to my watch supervisor and he to the watch officer, and so on.

Calls and decisions were made and two armed F-16s were launched to chase the suspect plane. For a brief time I tracked the F-16s as they caught up to the suspect and eventually forced it to land in Mexico. My commanding officer came in to CIC (Combat Information Center)and patted me on the back and began stroking egos with the other officers. A few hours later I went to CIC for my next watch. I was handed a message reporting on the incident I had previously instigated. It said that four people had been shot by the Mexican authorities. No weapons were found and NO drugs were found. Four innocent people murdered because of my actions.

At the time this happened I had less than a year to go on my enlistment. I was deciding whether or not to re-enlist. Up until this point I had pretty much decided to stay in. After this incident I couldn’t get out fast enough.

In the summer of 1992 an acquaintance introduced me to the Ohio Hempery www.hempery.com and ultimately the cannabis movement. I began reading everything I could on the topic. I became enthralled. I had smoked marijuana recreationally, but only a few times at this point. To me it was just a way to get high and party. The more I read the more this changed as well.

As I learned more about cannabis I kept remembering back to the four innocent people killed in Mexico. I was ashamed and felt I had to do something. I hate war. I was in the Persian Gulf in the late 80s, and though it wasn’t really a ‘war zone’ at the time, to a 20 year old from a small town in Indiana, it was hell.

Because of this I have become over the years a very outspoken proponent of drug law reform and cannabis legalization. At times I feel that it is my responsibility to do something to make up for the four lives that I feel responsible for ending. Yes, I was doing my job, but that is no excuse. I wasn’t drafted.

I have seen first hand the death and destruction caused by the Drug War, from both sides. Neither side is pretty. And it’s less attractive when it’s being done by the government to its own citizens. Despite what prohibitionists like to claim about the motivations of ‘legalizers;’ that we just want to get high, my motivations really have nothing to do with smoking marijuana. After experiencing what I have experienced I would still do this even if I had never smoked marijuana. This is not about dope, it’s about right and wrong.

Thank you,

Brad Manzenberger
BAMANZ@prodigy.net

P.S. I know that you post messages from readers from time to time. If you decide to please feel free and please post my name with it. I want everyone to know what REALLY goes on and I have nothing to hide from.
